title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 218: Harnessing the Gale: Wind-Powered Cargo
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 218 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

Harnessing the Gale: The Modern Revival of Wind-Powered Cargo

Paragraph 1. For over a century, international maritime shipping has depended heavily on fossil fuels. Colossal container ships and bulk carriers measuring up to four hundred metres long rely on giant low-speed diesel engines burning heavy fuel oil. While ocean shipping transports over eighty percent of world trade, the commercial fleet generates nearly three percent of global human-made greenhouse gases alongside heavy sulfur and soot emissions that harm coastal populations. Faced with strict net-zero targets from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), naval architects are reviving wind power through twenty-first-century aerospace design.

Paragraph 2. Modern wind-assisted ship propulsion (WASP) bears little resemblance to the canvas sails and wooden masts of nineteenth-century vessels. Instead, ships deploy rigid, computer-controlled structures resembling vertical airplane wings. Leading this shift is the 80,000-tonne dry bulk carrier Pyxis Ocean, fitted in 2023 with two composite WindWings standing 37.5 metres tall. Constructed from glass-fibre and carbon composites, each wing pairs a central spar with two movable flaps that rotate via autonomous algorithms to capture ocean winds at ideal angles.

Paragraph 3. During sea trials across the Indian and Atlantic Oceans, automated wings reduced daily fuel consumption by up to three tonnes, cutting carbon emissions by thirty percent. Equally important, supplemental aerodynamic thrust lets captains lower engine power without reducing cruising speed. This advantage shields maritime companies against sudden bunker fuel price spikes while noticeably extending the working lifespan of expensive engine parts.

Paragraph 4. However, retrofitting existing fleets involves major practical obstacles. One critical limitation is vertical clearance: cargo ships must pass safely through bottlenecks like the Panama and Suez Canals and dock beneath towering port gantry cranes exceeding thirty metres. To avoid collisions, naval engineers created hydraulic pivoting joints that fold the rigid wings flat against cargo hatchways in port. On the downside, the structural weight of this folding hardware trims the ship's maximum cargo load by several hundred tonnes.

Paragraph 5. To boost financial returns further, operators pair aerodynamic wings with intelligent voyage software. By reading real-time satellite weather data, currents, and wave drag, algorithms chart dynamic routes through wind-rich ocean corridors rather than sticking to fixed straight shipping lanes. Although detours can add extra nautical miles, the fuel saved by steady tailwinds far outweighs the longer distance.

Paragraph 6. Beyond rigid wings, shipyards are actively testing spinning cylindrical Flettner rotors and autonomous towing kites to suit different vessel sizes. Together, these innovations show that the oldest energy source in maritime history may offer the fastest, most practical route toward zero-carbon global shipping.

groups.title: Questions 9–12
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.

q1.text: How do modern WindWings differ from nineteenth-century clipper sails?
options: A. They are stitched from waterproof woollen cloth.
B. They are powered purely by underwater propellers.
C. They are detached manually before entering open seas.
D. They are rigid composite structures inspired by aircraft.

steps: Đoạn 2: Cấu trúc cánh cứng bằng composite giống cánh máy bay dựng đứng.

q2.text: What was achieved during sea trials across the Indian and Atlantic Oceans?
options: A. Daily fuel use and carbon output dropped substantially.
B. Cruising speeds doubled without touching the sails.
C. Main diesel engines were removed permanently.
D. Port loading times fell by thirty percent.

steps: Đoạn 3: Giảm tới 3 tấn dầu mỗi ngày và giảm 30% khí thải carbon.

q3.text: Why could rigid sails exceeding 30 metres cause serious problems at ports?
options: A. They block sunlight from reaching harbour offices.
B. They make ships float too high above dock walls.
C. They risk colliding with overhead gantry cranes and bridges.
D. They prevent cargo crews from opening side doors.

steps: Đoạn 4: Có nguy cơ va chạm với cẩu giàn cảng biển và cầu.

q4.text: Why do dynamic routing algorithms sometimes pick slightly longer ocean paths?
options: A. To avoid paying fees along the Suez Canal
B. Because wind-rich routes generate net energy savings
C. Because satellite telemetry cannot read straight shipping lanes
D. To give engine mechanics extra hours for repairs

steps: Đoạn 5: Dù thêm hải lý, lực đẩy gió ổn định giúp tiết kiệm nhiên liệu ròng lớn hơn.

q9.text: International shipping currently produces over ten percent of global greenhouse gases.

steps: Đoạn 1: Ngành tàu biển thải ra gần 3% (nearly three percent), không phải trên 10%.

q10.text: Flettner rotors have proven three times more effective than rigid WindWings.

steps: Đoạn 6: Chỉ nói đang thử nghiệm rô-to Flettner và diều kéo, không so sánh hiệu quả gấp 3 lần.

q11.text: Using wind propulsion helps mechanical engine components last longer.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...noticeably extending the working lifespan of expensive engine parts."

q12.text: Dynamic routing software always forces vessels to follow the shortest geographic line.

steps: Đoạn 5: Phần mềm chủ động đi vòng qua hành lang gió thay vì bám tuyến đường thẳng ngắn nhất.
